scope: Individual full stored transcript and actual image review

title.analysis: Exact: "Why Buying A House In 2026 Is A Financial Trap" (46 characters, 10 words). The first five words identify the decision and year; "financial trap" is a clear negative declaration with urgency, loss aversion and browse curiosity. Search terms are buying a house, 2026 and financial trap. It promises a general warning rather than a local decision model, so it overstates a conditional transcript that ultimately gives five circumstances where buying can make sense. The title contains no amount, unlike stronger and weaker house-affordability comparators.
title.search_demand: Historical Google Trends series unavailable. VERIFIED_DEMAND context: 2025 Bankrate evidence found renting cheaper on its short-term method in all 50 largest metros, while NAR reported a record-low 21% first-time-buyer share and median age 40. Frozen outcomes do not show a universal title formula: target 0.80526 TYPICAL; same-pool when-to-buy 0.70636 TYPICAL and $750K affordability 0.56895 TYPICAL; older identical $500K affordability titles range from 23.00921 STRONG to 0.34643 WEAK.
title.script_alignment: High message alignment: the script argues that buying at current national prices and rates can be a trap, the thumbnail literalizes the trap, and the conclusion says rent when local math says rent. The unqualified title and thumbnail omit the script's later local-market, holding-period, liquidity and lifestyle exceptions.

thumbnail.analysis: Actual 1280x720 and 320x180 inspected. White background; large frightened cartoon man at left; bold black "IT'S A TRAP.." at upper right; curved black arrow; and a gray bear trap with red glow enclosing a suburban house and $500K sign. Six principal visual elements remain legible at mobile size. Face, text and trap form a left-to-right hierarchy; high black/white contrast and red danger halo convey fear immediately. The $500K sign adds a price point absent from the title and transcript's $400K worked case. The literal trap closely matches the title but visually suppresses the conditional ending and can imply all $500K houses are traps. No historical snapshot proves this was the served creative throughout the frozen metric window.

script.analysis: All 20,133 canonical stored characters read in five verified contiguous ranges. Cold open follows fictional pre-approved buyers Lucas and Michelle at a late-night kitchen table; calculator discovery supplies conflict before the thesis. Progression: national affordability and price-to-income context; $400K purchase amortization; insurance, maintenance, property-tax and Florida-condo risks; Bankrate rent-versus-buy comparison; renter investment and owner terminal-value scenarios; Shiller/stock history; industry incentives and unrecoverable costs; mortgage-interest deduction; five conditions for buying; first-time-buyer context; Lucas/Michelle optionality payoff and CTA. The recurring couple provides continuity, rehooks and a circular close. Direct mechanisms and vivid examples improve clarity, but the central comparison mixes nominal and real assumptions and repeatedly generalizes national averages to individual decisions. The stored captions omit the property-tax number in the first monthly-cost calculation; original audio and timing are unverified.

claim_audit: 0:5000 The $320,000, 6.3%, 30-year amortization recalculates to $1,980.71 monthly, $1,680 first-month interest, $300.71 first-month principal, $393,056.65 total interest and $713,056.65 total principal plus interest; principal first exceeds interest in payment 229, about 19.08 years. Those core figures are accurate. The captions omit the property-tax number, but $366.67 monthly tax plus stated insurance and HOA reconciles the stated $2,785 total. Calling $80,000 roughly top 5% liquid cash is uncited and depends on unit/population. National median-price, rate and Atlanta Fed context are publication-window evidence, not a local affordability result.

5000:10000 The strongest regulatory claim is directionally supported: Florida law restricts waiving required structural-integrity reserves for covered associations, but the operative budget restriction began after December 31, 2024, not simply January 2026, and statutory exceptions/funding methods matter. The $180K/$400K Aventura assessment examples were not reproduced from an identified primary record. NAIC evidence reviewed supports large premium increases but not the transcript's exact national 46% since 2021; a cited 2021-2024 analysis found 24%, while Florida estimates vary by modeled policy. Bankrate did report $2,768 versus $2,000 and a 38% gap in all 50 large metros, but compared average rents for all homes with payments on a median-priced home under standardized assumptions, not necessarily comparable properties; it excluded maintenance, closing costs, equity, refinancing and tax benefits.

10000:15000 With $80K initially and $500 monthly at 7% effective real return, recalculated values are about $242.9K/$563.3K/$1.194M after 10/20/30 years, close to the script's $244K/$570K/$1.22M. The model calls the monthly saving $500-$800 but reports approximately the $500 path. The owner scenario's $400K growing 3% for 30 years gives $970.9K and $883.5K after 9% selling costs, also close. The comparison is not like-for-like: stocks use 7% real while the house uses 3% nominal, ownership expenses are largely held flat, rent growth is omitted, and stock taxes/fees and housing tax benefits/leverage/local variation are not modeled. The roughly $1.21M owner outlay is arithmetically reproducible only with fixed annual costs and does not transparently add purchase closing costs despite naming them. The Bankrate study itself warns that its short-term comparison does not include several of these items. Therefore "in most scenarios" is not established by this single model.

10000:15000 The year-one unrecoverable-cost sum is about $34,260 using $20,160 interest, $4,400 tax, $2,400 insurance, $4,000 maintenance and $3,300 HOA, so its narrow arithmetic works. Insurance is stated earlier as $167 monthly (about $2,004 annually), creating a $396 inconsistency. Nine-percent selling costs are an assumption, not a universal post-settlement fee. The claims that commissions rose after the NAR settlement and that NAR's culture/marketing caused the American dream are not established here. IRS guidance confirms mortgage interest requires itemizing and is subject to debt and use limits; it does not make the transcript's broad causal characterization of the tax code.

15000:20133 Price-to-rent under 15, seven-to-ten-year holding, 20% down, 28% all-in gross income and a house under 30% of net worth are heuristics rather than universal rules; the net-worth rule also mixes a gross house value with an unspecified wealth measure. NAR's 2025 survey verifies a 21% first-time-buyer share and median age 40 for transactions July 2024-June 2025. The script's final "bubble ... deflating" forecast is a hypothesis and sits uneasily beside its opening observation of 33 consecutive months of year-over-year price gains. Lock-in, insurance withdrawal and unaffordability can constrain supply or demand without proving that recent buyers will bear an inevitable deflation.

topic.analysis: Owner-occupied buy-versus-rent decision under 2026 affordability conditions, aimed at prospective first-time buyers with enough income/down payment to consider purchasing but worried about rates, hidden costs and lost flexibility. Primary motivations are fear, security, savings and relief from status pressure. The decision framework is evergreen; the price, mortgage-rate, insurance, tax-law and Florida-condo evidence is news-sensitive. VERIFIED_DEMAND: publication-window NAR/Atlanta-Fed/Bankrate evidence supports severe affordability and low first-time participation. CONTEXT_ONLY: national averages do not decide a local household's rent-versus-buy outcome. PLAUSIBLE_HYPOTHESIS: fear framing and a worked couple may broaden appeal. UNAVAILABLE: historical Google Trends/search volume and private recommendation exposure.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: A stronger original treatment would publish a transparent local calculator with matched property quality, nominal-or-real consistency, rent growth, taxes, insurance, maintenance, transaction costs, investment taxes/fees, time horizon and sensitivity ranges. Separate owner-occupied lifestyle value from investment-property returns and show break-even years rather than a universal trap claim.

virality.analysis: 6,667 frozen public views at 125.1489 days, 23:22; 0.80526x TYPICAL against 10 same-channel LONG_FORM age peers, stable at 0.67074x TYPICAL in the saved five-peer sensitivity check. The exact pool contains STRONG lifestyle-exposure 2.49527 and $10K-to-$500K 2.18248, TYPICAL neighbor-broke 1.30728, rent-affordability 1.06668, lazy habits 0.9092, banks/wealth 0.90647, target 0.80526, creator-income 0.68148, house affordability 0.70636 and $750K affordability 0.56895, plus WEAK insurance/income 0.30227. The target's large mobile-legible fear packaging, timely affordability evidence and continuous couple narrative did not produce a breakout. Broader housing outcomes span STRONG, TYPICAL and WEAK with identical or closely related formulas, contradicting a universal "house + shocking math/trap" winner. Topic breadth, channel timing, distribution, audience saturation and unknown recommendation exposure remain alternatives; private CTR, impressions, retention and satisfaction are unavailable.

original_content_lesson.test: Test a local, transparent rent-versus-buy calculator video against a matched fear-framed version. Keep nominal/real bases consistent, publish every assumption, show break-even sensitivity by hold period and price-to-rent ratio, and measure own CTR, first-30-second retention, calculator-section retention, traffic sources and post-view comprehension.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH that fear packaging and housing topic are not sufficient for breakout in this corpus; LOW on the causal reason for this video's typical result
